caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: CRCNS:stc-1
attempts.entry_title: Perceptual learning and noise correlations in MSTd (Gu et al. 2011)
attempts.summary: The main finding holds: MSTd noise correlations are lower in trained than in naive monkeys (0.024 against 0.119), and training lowers the relation between noise and signal correlation without changing its slope, though the intercept intervals overlap. The population simulations also hold, with correlated noise limiting sensitivity and the trained reduction changing it little, but narrowing preferences gives a smaller gain than reported, under tuning parameters the paper does not state. Smaller choice probabilities in fore-aft neurons did not reproduce, on 129 units from two trained monkeys that may not be the paper's sample. Time courses, Fano factors and naive against trained single-neuron tuning could not be tested, as the data set holds no spike times or naive single units.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Gu, Liu, Fetsch, Yang, Fok, Sunkara, DeAngelis and Angelaki (2011) on CRCNS stc-1, which holds the noise and signal correlations and preferred headings of the paper's 127 MSTd pairs under 1 mm, and single-unit tuning and choice probabilities of two trained monkeys. It compares noise correlations between naive and trained animals, their relation to signal correlation, and the paper's population simulations. Analyses that need spike times, distances or the single-electrode database cannot be run on it.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Gu et al. (2011) from CRCNS stc-1

outcomes.statement: The monkeys of the data set's 127 MSTd pairs can be assigned to the paper's naive and trained groups, and the assignment agrees with what the data set and the paper both describe.
outcomes.source: Figure S2B legend; Experimental Procedures, Experimental Protocol and Task, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: 4 subjects (with n= 35, 26, 18, and 8 pairs) were trained in the heading discrimination task (red curves) and 3 animals (with n= 22, 11 and 5 pairs) were naïve (blue curves). Data from one trained animal with only two pairs of neurons is not shown.
outcomes.notes: Monkeys are matched by their number of pairs. The eight counts in the data (35, 26, 22, 18, 11, 8, 5, 2) equal the eight of the Figure S2B legend, all distinct, so the match is one to one, with monkeys 19, 18, 2, 5 and 24 trained and 17, 1 and 3 naive. It gives 89 trained and 38 naive pairs, and 146 trained and 64 naive units (units told apart within a recording by their preferred headings), as the paper and the Figure 3 legend state. Monkeys 2 and 5, whose heading discrimination thresholds the data set holds in experiment 2, are trained.
deviations: The data set has no training-group label; the groups come from the paper's per-animal counts.

outcomes.statement: Mean noise correlation among MSTd pairs (separated by less than 1 mm) is significantly smaller in trained animals (0.023 +- 0.017 SEM, n = 89) than in naive animals (0.116 +- 0.031, n = 38).
outcomes.source: Results, Comparison of Noise Correlations in Trained and Naive Animals, paragraph 2; Figure 2B
outcomes.quote: The mean noise correlation in the trained group (0.023 ± 0.017 SEM, n = 89) was significantly smaller than that for naive animals (0.116 ± 0.031, n = 38, p = 0.006, t test)
outcomes.notes: Trained 0.0241 +- 0.0174 SEM (n = 89), naive 0.1190 +- 0.0316 (n = 38), both within the reported SEMs; Student t test p = 0.0056 (paper 0.006), Welch p = 0.0108. Visual rnoise alone gives p = 0.0047, vestibular alone p = 0.071. Without the trained animal with two pairs, p = 0.0032.
deviations: Assumed that the pooled rnoise is the mean of the vestibular and visual rnoise. The data set holds only the per-condition values; the Experimental Procedures (Noise and Signal Correlations, paragraph 2) pool the z-scored responses across conditions, and the correlation of pooled z-scores is the trial-weighted mean of the per-condition correlations, with equal weights when the conditions are interleaved with equal repetitions (Experimental Protocol and Task). Outlier removal could make the weights differ slightly.
Whether the stored values include the renormalization in blocks of 20 trials cannot be told, and the reading with the other choice cannot be run, as the data set holds no trial responses.
Training groups from the link claim.

outcomes.statement: The greater noise correlation in naive animals holds for individual animals; four trained animals (35, 26, 18 and 8 pairs) and three naive animals (22, 11 and 5 pairs) are shown, and the difference is consistent across animals within each group.
outcomes.source: Results, Comparison of Noise Correlations in Trained and Naive Animals, paragraph 3; Figure S2B; Discussion, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Importantly, these observations held true when correlations were examined for individual animals
outcomes.notes: Pair counts 35, 26, 18, 8 (trained shown) and 22, 11, 5 (naive) match the legend. Every naive animal mean (0.0876 to 0.2545) exceeds every trained animal mean among those shown (-0.0449 to 0.0484). The trained animal with two pairs, not shown in the paper, has a mean of 0.2708. The per-animal time courses of Figure S2B need spike times and are not tested.
deviations: Pooled rnoise as the mean of the two conditions (assumption, as in fig2b).
Means over the middle 1 s only; the figure shows time courses.

outcomes.statement: For the example pair of Figure 1, signal correlation is 0.83 (visual) and 0.79 (vestibular), and noise correlation is 0.29 (visual, p = 0.04) and 0.14 (vestibular, p = 0.3).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraphs 1 and 2; Figure 1B to 1E
outcomes.quote: For this example pair of neurons, rsignal = 0.83 and 0.79 for the visual and vestibular conditions, respectively ... rnoise = 0.29, p = 0.04, Figure 1D ... R = 0.14, p = 0.3, Figure 1E

statistics.about: rnoise of the example pair, visual
rnoise of the example pair, vestibular

outcomes.notes: Pair m2c338r1 (monkey 2, trained) has all four values within tolerance; no other pair has more than two. The per-pair p values (0.04 and 0.3) need trial counts, which the data set does not hold, so that part of the statement is not tested.

outcomes.statement: Noise correlations computed from visual and vestibular responses are correlated across pairs (R = 0.38, p << 0.001, Spearman rank correlation, 179 pairs).
outcomes.source: Results, Noise Correlations in Area MSTd, paragraph 2; Figure 1F
outcomes.quote: Noise correlations computed from visual and vestibular responses were significantly correlated across 179 pairs of neurons (R = 0.38, p << 0.001, Spearman rank correlation)
outcomes.notes: Spearman R = 0.449, p = 1.2e-07, over 127 pairs; positive and significant, but outside 0.342 to 0.418. Trained 0.395 (n = 89), naive 0.480 (n = 38).
deviations: The 127 pairs under 1 mm, the criterion's second reading; the paper's 179 are not in the data set.

outcomes.statement: Mean noise correlation does not differ between the vestibular (0.035 +- 0.014 SEM) and visual (0.039 +- 0.015) conditions (p > 0.8, paired t test).
outcomes.source: Results, Noise Correlations in Area MSTd, paragraph 2; Figure 1F
outcomes.quote: their means were not significantly different (vestibular ... 0.035 ± 0.014 SEM, visual ... 0.039 ± 0.015, p > 0.8, paired t test)
outcomes.notes: Paired t = 0.346, p = 0.730, n = 127; mean difference 0.0068, 95% CI -0.032 to 0.046. The vestibular mean (0.0559 +- 0.0173) is outside 0.035 +- 0.014; the visual mean (0.0491 +- 0.0199) is inside 0.039 +- 0.015.
deviations: The 127 pairs under 1 mm, not the paper's 179.

outcomes.statement: Noise correlation increases with signal correlation in both conditions (vestibular p = 0.0001, visual p = 0.0004, ANCOVA).
outcomes.source: Results, Training Effects on the Noise-Signal Correlation Structure, paragraph 1; Figures 5A and 5B
outcomes.quote: There was a significant positive correlation between rnoise and rsignal in both stimulus conditions (vestibular ... p = 0.0001; visual ... p = 0.0004, ANCOVA)
outcomes.notes: With pooled rnoise the rsignal term has vestibular p = 0.00017 and visual p = 0.00070 (Type II, model with interaction; the additive model gives 0.00016 and 0.00066), slopes 0.130 and 0.105. With the same-condition rnoise p = 0.00009 and 0.017. Per monkey, the slopes are positive in 12 of 14 monkey and condition cells; the two negative ones are monkey 3 (5 pairs).
deviations: Pooled rnoise as the mean of the two conditions (assumption, as in fig2b).
The paper does not say how the ANCOVA sums of squares are formed; Type II tests with and without the interaction are shown and agree.

outcomes.statement: Training does not change the slope of the relation between noise and signal correlation (vestibular p = 0.9, visual p = 0.9, ANCOVA interaction).
outcomes.source: Results, Training Effects on the Noise-Signal Correlation Structure, paragraph 2; Figure 5C
outcomes.quote: the slope of the relationship between rnoise and rsignal (Figures 5A and 5B) was not significantly affected by training (vestibular ... p = 0.9; visual ... p = 0.9, ANCOVA interaction effect)
outcomes.notes: Interaction p = 0.830 (vestibular) and 0.962 (visual) with pooled rnoise; 0.630 and 0.894 with the same-condition rnoise. Slopes, vestibular, naive 0.119 (95% CI -0.021 to 0.259) and trained 0.135 (0.060 to 0.210); visual, naive 0.107 (-0.026 to 0.240) and trained 0.104 (0.038 to 0.170).
deviations: Pooled rnoise as the mean of the two conditions (assumption, as in fig2b).

outcomes.statement: Training lowers noise correlation uniformly across signal correlations, a main effect of training (vestibular p = 0.02, visual p = 0.008, ANCOVA) with non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals of the intercepts.
outcomes.source: Results, Training Effects on the Noise-Signal Correlation Structure, paragraph 2; Figure 5D
outcomes.quote: training had a significant main effect on rnoise (vestibular ... p = 0.02; visual; p = 0.008 ANCOVA), and the 95% confidence intervals around the regression intercepts were non-overlapping for naive and trained animals
outcomes.notes: The training main effect holds with pooled rnoise (vestibular p = 0.0184, visual p = 0.0074; paper 0.02 and 0.008), with higher naive intercepts (0.095 against 0.015, 0.096 against 0.009). The 95% intervals of the intercepts overlap under every reading. Vestibular, separate fits give naive 0.026 to 0.163 and trained -0.018 to 0.048; the ANCOVA model gives 0.036 to 0.153 and -0.020 to 0.050. Visual is alike, as is the additive model. Bootstrap intervals of each group's own fit (2000 resamples of pairs within the group) also overlap, vestibular naive 0.040 to 0.151 and trained -0.016 to 0.046, visual 0.021 to 0.172 and -0.023 to 0.040. With the same-condition rnoise the vestibular main effect is not significant (p = 0.183).
deviations: Pooled rnoise as the mean of the two conditions (assumption, as in fig2b).

The paper does not say how the intercept intervals of Figure 5D were computed; separate per-group fits, the ANCOVA model with interaction (Figure 5 legend, "regression fits (ANCOVA)"), the additive model and a bootstrap over pairs are all shown, and all overlap.

outcomes.statement: The plane fitted to noise and the two signal correlations is rnoise = 0.12 rsignal,vestibular + 0.091 rsignal,visual + 0.072 in naive animals, with the same slopes and an intercept of 0.005 in trained animals.
outcomes.source: Results, Computation of Covariance Matrix, paragraph 2; Experimental Procedures, Population Coding, equation 5
outcomes.inferred: Read from the equations of the Results, whose multiplication sign the extracted text prints as "3"; no sentence states the values in words.
outcomes.notes: Reading (a) gives slopes 0.119 and 0.084 and naive intercept 0.077, within tolerance, and trained intercept 0.0034, outside 0.005 +- 0.0005 (bootstrap 95% interval -0.026 to 0.035). Reading (b) gives 0.132, 0.085, 0.074 and 0.0024; reading (c) puts the visual slope (0.106) outside tolerance. No reading has all four within tolerance; the slopes match and the naive intercept exceeds the trained one under (a) and (b). Separate orthogonal fits per group give naive 0.123, 0.106 and 0.071 and a trained intercept of 0.0046, close to the paper's equations but with different slopes per group, which is not a reading of the criterion.
deviations: Pooled rnoise as the mean of the two conditions (assumption, as in fig2b).

outcomes.statement: In simulated populations, correlated noise as measured in naive animals raises the population threshold about 5-fold over independent noise at 2000 neurons, while the uniform reduction in trained animals has little effect on the threshold compared with naive.
outcomes.source: Results, Effect of Training on Population Coding Efficiency, paragraphs 1 and 2; Figure 6A
outcomes.quote: For a simulated population of 2000 neurons, the predicted heading discrimination threshold was ... larger compared with the case of independent noise. Surprisingly, the uniform reduction in rnoise that we observed in trained animals (Figure 5) had little effect on predicted discrimination thresholds, as compared with naive animals
outcomes.notes: At 2000 neurons the naive threshold is 5.41 times the independent one, and trained is within 0.01% of naive, under both rsignal readings, which give the same values because their rsignal differs by at most 5.6e-07; the open parameters that matter are the amplitude and baseline. The ratio is 4.32 to 5.90 over the amplitude and baseline variants, and 9.18 without the trace term of equation 3. With the coefficients fitted here (reading c) it is 5.47.
deviations: Tuning amplitude 30 spikes/s, baseline 10 spikes/s and a 1 s count are the claims file's readings; the paper does not give them, and the ratio depends on them.
Preferences evenly spaced on the circle, a standard choice for the legend's "uniformly distributed".

outcomes.statement: Population thresholds (256 neurons) are very sensitive to the slope of the relation between noise and signal correlation and only weakly sensitive to its intercept; a uniform increase in rnoise lowers the threshold slightly.
outcomes.source: Results, Effect of Training on Population Coding Efficiency, paragraph 2; Figure 6B
outcomes.quote: predicted thresholds were very sensitive to changes in the slope of the relationship between rnoise and rsignal. In contrast, changes in the intercept of the rnoise versus rsignal relationship had weak effects on predicted thresholds
outcomes.notes: At 256 neurons a slope change of 0.2 around the measured 0.211 changes the threshold by 1.97 degrees (naive intercept) and 1.93 (trained), an intercept change over 0 to 0.2 at the measured slope by 0.11. The threshold falls as the intercept rises from 0.02 to 0.2 (7.254 to 7.107) and from the trained to the naive intercept (7.251 to 7.217), with a small rise from 0 to 0.02 (7.220 to 7.254).
deviations: Tuning parameters as in fig6a (claims file readings, not from the paper).
The slope axis is taken as the sum of the two slopes, the slope on rsignal when tuning is congruent, as the Results assume for the simulations.

outcomes.statement: For a single pair of neurons, reducing noise correlation lowers the discrimination threshold when signal correlation is positive and raises it when signal correlation is negative.
outcomes.source: Results, Effect of Training on Population Coding Efficiency, paragraph 3; Figure 7A; Figure S7A
outcomes.quote: reducing the noise correlation between this pair of neurons results in a lower population threshold (red curve below blue curve) when the pair of neurons has positive rsignal. In contrast, reducing noise correlation increases the predicted threshold for negative rsignal
outcomes.notes: Trained is lower than naive for all 88 pairs with positive rsignal and higher for 92 of 93 with negative rsignal. The exception, at rsignal = -0.011, has trained 0.09% below naive; the ratio of trained to naive crosses 1 at rsignal = -0.0216, between second preferences of -1 and -2 degrees. The criterion asks for every pair.
deviations: Tuning parameters as in fig6a (claims file readings, not from the paper).

outcomes.statement: In a 256-neuron population, narrowing heading preferences to give more pairs with positive signal correlation (49%, 75%, 94%) makes the weaker noise correlations of trained animals improve coding, but at best the trained threshold is about 8% lower than the naive.
outcomes.source: Results, Effect of Training on Population Coding Efficiency, paragraph 4; Figure 7C; Figure S7B
outcomes.quote: At best, however, the predicted population discrimination threshold for trained animals is ... lower than for naive animals
outcomes.notes: The proportions of positive rsignal are within tolerance. The trained improvement grows from -0.48% to 4.83% as the range narrows and then levels off (4.58% to 4.83%); its maximum, 4.83%, is below 8 +- 0.8%. The maximum is 3.6% to 6.0% under the amplitude and baseline variants and 11.75% without the trace term of equation 3. Two of the criterion's three parts hold (the improvement grows as the range narrows; the proportions are within tolerance) and the best improvement is smaller than the paper's, so the effect is present but weaker. Recorded as not_reproduced before the round-1 verification and changed to partially_reproduced, as the verifier proposed.
deviations: Tuning parameters as in fig6a (claims file readings, not from the paper); the result depends on them and on the trace term.
Ranges centred on 90 degrees with widths 360 to 10 degrees, containing the legend's [0, 180] and [30, 150]; the figure's other ranges are not given in the text.

outcomes.statement: Neurons preferring fore-aft headings have smaller choice probabilities than neurons preferring lateral headings (p = 0.019, t test), and choice probability does not differ between neurons preferring leftward and rightward headings (p = 0.11).
outcomes.source: Results, Possible rsignal Distributions in Area MSTd, paragraphs 2 and 3; Figures 8A and 8B
outcomes.quote: neurons with a preference for fore-aft movement show significantly smaller choice probabilities (p = 0.019, t test, Figures 8A and 8B) ... there was no significant difference in average choice probability between neurons preferring leftward and rightward headings (p = 0.11, t test)

statistics.n: 311 single-electrode recordings, vestibular and visual pooled

outcomes.notes: On 258 values from 129 units of monkeys 2 and 5, fore-aft units do not have smaller choice probabilities. With spline-peak preferences, fore-aft 0.527 against lateral 0.542, p = 0.136. With the weighted vector sum, 0.533 against 0.535, p = 0.796. Leftward and rightward units do not differ under any reading (p = 0.25 to 0.35), as the paper says. Variants, the vector sum over the 8 evenly spaced headings gives p = 0.691, and the distance of CP from 0.5 gives p = 0.10 to 0.17. The vector sum and spline readings put 71.7% of values in the same group. Of the CPs 71.7% are above 0.5 (mean 0.534), consistent with CPs signed relative to each unit's preferred direction. The round-1 version used an unweighted vector sum, biased toward straight ahead by the uneven headings, which gave p = 0.0006 in the opposite direction; it was replaced.
deviations: A subset of the paper's data. The data set holds the choice probabilities of 129 units of two trained monkeys from Gu et al. (2008), 258 values over the two conditions, against the paper's 311; whether they are among the 311 cannot be checked.
Preferred headings from the experiment 1 tuning curves of the same cells, by the two readings of the claims file; the data set does not say how its CPs are signed.

The experiment 1 headings are unevenly spaced (+-22.5 degrees added to the eight 45 degrees apart), so the vector sum weights each response by half the gaps to its two neighbours. On synthetic curves this recovers the preference to within 3 degrees, where the unweighted sum puts 30 degrees at 16. A choice made here, after the round-1 verification.

outcomes.statement: Noise correlation does not depend significantly on heading preference (p = 0.2, t test); lateral neurons have slightly smaller noise correlations than fore-aft neurons.
outcomes.source: Results, Possible rsignal Distributions in Area MSTd, paragraph 3; Figures 8C and 8D
outcomes.quote: there was no significant ... dependence of noise correlation on the heading preferences of MSTd neurons (p = 0.2, t test)

statistics.n: 328 fixation and 55 discrimination-task points, each pair plotted at both neurons' preferences

outcomes.notes: Over the 178 points of the trained pairs under 1 mm, lateral against fore-aft p = 0.434 with visual preferences (0.033 against 0.014) and p = 0.170 with vestibular preferences (0.011 against 0.045). Lateral is lower only with vestibular preferences. Variant with all 127 pairs (254 points), vestibular preferences give a significant difference (0.022 against 0.096, p = 0.0009), visual do not (p = 0.623). The variant's 254 points are nearer the legend's 328 than the 178 used, so by point count alone the claims file's rule would judge on it, and the claim would then fail with vestibular preferences. The outcome is kept on the trained pairs, a complete reading of the criterion and the sample the Results name ("in trained animals"); the 127 pairs are the all-179 reading with the 52 pairs over 1 mm missing.
deviations: Of the claims file's readings only the trained pairs under 1 mm can be formed (178 points, the legend has 328 and 55); the other trained pairs, the pairs over 1 mm and the task points are not in the data set.
Pooled rnoise as the mean of the two conditions (assumption, as in fig2b); preferred headings as stored in the data set, whose method is not described.

outcomes.statement: Noise correlation is greater in naive than in trained animals throughout the time course of the response, computed in 500 ms windows stepped by 50 ms (p = 0.002, permutation test).
outcomes.source: Results, Comparison of Noise Correlations in Trained and Naive Animals, paragraph 3; Figure 2C
outcomes.quote: rnoise was significantly greater in naive than trained animals throughout the time course of the neural response (p = 0.002, permutation test, see Experimental Procedures)
outcomes.notes: Needs spike times in 500 ms windows. The data set (stc-1/live, MSTd.mat, VIP.mat, demo.m and the docs) holds one noise correlation per pair and condition, no spike times or trial responses.

outcomes.statement: The difference in rnoise between naive and trained animals is largest at the beginning of the trial and decreases with time (Spearman R = -0.9, p << 0.001).
outcomes.source: Results, Comparison of Noise Correlations in Trained and Naive Animals, paragraph 3; Figure S2A
outcomes.quote: The difference in rnoise between naive and trained animals was largest at the beginning of the trial and gradually decreased with time
outcomes.notes: Depends on fig2c-timecourse-naive-higher; no spike times in the data set.

outcomes.statement: The time course of the population average response to the preferred heading does not differ between trained (n = 146 neurons) and naive (n = 64) animals (p = 0.8, permutation test).
outcomes.source: Results, Effects of Training on Tuning Curves, Variability, and Sensitivity of Single Neurons, paragraph 1; Figures 3A and 3C
outcomes.quote: the time course of the populationaverage response to the preferred heading was indistinguishable between trained and naive animals (p = 0.8, permutation test
outcomes.notes: Needs spike times of the pair units; the data set holds none.

outcomes.statement: Training has no significant effect on the time course of the Fano factor (p = 0.5, permutation test).
outcomes.source: Results, Effects of Training on Tuning Curves, Variability, and Sensitivity of Single Neurons, paragraph 1; Figures 3B and 3D; Figure S3
outcomes.quote: There was also no significant effect (p = 0.5, permutation test) of training on the time course of the Fano factor
outcomes.notes: Needs spike counts per trial and window; the data set holds none.

outcomes.statement: Renormalizing responses in blocks of 20 trials has no significant effect on noise correlations (R = 0.9 before against after), and the effect does not differ between naive and trained animals (interaction p = 0.7, group p = 0.9, ANCOVA).
outcomes.source: Experimental Procedures, Noise and Signal Correlations, paragraph 2; Figure S8C
outcomes.quote: This additional normalization had no significant effect on rnoise (p > 0.3, paired t test; R = 0.9, p < < 0.001, Spearman rank correlation, n = 127, Figure S8). More importantly, the effect of renormalization on noise correlations was similar in naive and trained animals (p = 0.7, interaction effect, p = 0.9, group effect, ANCOVA, Figure S8)
outcomes.notes: Needs trial-ordered responses to renormalize; the data set holds one value per pair and condition, without saying whether it includes the renormalization.

outcomes.statement: Noise correlations decrease in the presence of the stimulus compared with prestimulus baseline activity.
outcomes.source: Discussion, Properties of Noise Correlations in MSTd, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: we observed that noise correlations decrease in the presence of a stimulus as compared with prestimulus baseline activity
outcomes.notes: Needs prestimulus spike counts; the data set holds none.

outcomes.statement: Noise correlations depend on distance; mean rnoise is above zero for pairs under 0.05 mm (0.042 +- 0.021, p = 0.049, n = 67) and 0.05 to 1 mm (0.062 +- 0.024, p = 0.011, n = 60), but not for pairs over 1 mm (0 +- 0.15, p = 0.9, n = 52).
outcomes.source: Results, Noise Correlations in Area MSTd, paragraph 3; Figure S1
outcomes.quote: Average noise correlations were significantly greater than zero for the first two groups (<0.05 mm ... 0.042 ± 0.021 SEM, p = 0.049, t test; 0.05-1 mm ... 0.062 ± 0.024, p = 0.011), but not for the group of distant pairs (>1 mm ... 0 ± 0.15, p = 0.9)
outcomes.notes: The data set holds only the 127 pairs under 1 mm, none of the 52 pairs over 1 mm, and no distance or electrode label, so neither the third group nor the split of the first two can be formed.

outcomes.statement: Noise correlations do not differ significantly between pairs recorded on one electrode (0.042 +- 0.02) and on different electrodes (0.033 +- 0.015), p > 0.7, t test.
outcomes.source: Experimental Procedures, Electrophysiological Recordings, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: noise correlations were slightly greater for pairs of neurons recorded from a single electrode (0.042 ± 0.02) than for pairs recorded from different electrodes (0.033 ± 0.015), this difference was modest and not significant (p > 0.7, t test)
outcomes.notes: No pair carries an electrode label. Ten pairs of monkey 17, in six recordings, have file_ids ending in "s", which the data descriptor does not explain (printed under the data check); the paper's 67 single-electrode pairs cannot be identified. The 52 pairs over 1 mm, needed for the reading over all 179 pairs, are not in the data set either.

outcomes.statement: Heading discrimination thresholds of the five trained monkeys were high (over 10 degrees) early in training and decreased gradually to a plateau of 1 to 3 degrees.
outcomes.source: Results, Comparison of Noise Correlations in Trained and Naive Animals, paragraph 1; Figure 2A
outcomes.quote: These monkeys' heading discrimination thresholds (corresponding to 84% correct) were high ... at early stages of training, and gradually decreased to a plateau of only a few degrees
outcomes.notes: The training histories are not in the data set. Experiment 2 holds one threshold per animal for two of the five trained monkeys (vestibular 1.2 and 3.1 degrees, both inside 0.9 to 3.3; visual 1.2 and 3.25 degrees), not the thresholds over sessions the criterion fits. Whether these are plateau values, and the fall from above 10 degrees, cannot be checked. The notebook states them under the data check.

outcomes.statement: Median visual tuning width does not differ between naive (124.5 degrees) and trained (126 degrees) animals (p = 0.21, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
outcomes.source: Results, Effects of Training on Tuning Curves, Variability, and Sensitivity of Single Neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 4A
outcomes.quote: There was no significant difference in median tuning width for the visual condition
outcomes.notes: The single-electrode database of 992 and 556 neurons is not in the data set. Experiment 1 holds the tuning curves of 129 units of two trained monkeys only, so naive and trained cannot be compared.

outcomes.statement: Median vestibular tuning width is slightly larger in trained (131 degrees) than in naive (121 degrees) animals (p = 0.045).
outcomes.source: Results, Effects of Training on Tuning Curves, Variability, and Sensitivity of Single Neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 4E
outcomes.quote: The difference in median tuning width was significant for the vestibular condition
outcomes.notes: As fig4-tuning-width-visual.

outcomes.statement: Training has no significant effect on tuning curve amplitude, visual (naive 35.4 against trained 31.8 spikes/s, p = 0.24) or vestibular (17.4 against 17.2 spikes/s, p = 0.36).
outcomes.source: Results, Effects of Training on Tuning Curves, Variability, and Sensitivity of Single Neurons, paragraph 2; Figures 4B and 4F
outcomes.quote: training did not have any significant effect on the distribution of tuning curve amplitudes in either the visual condition (naive ... 35.4 spks/s versus trained ... 31.8 spks/s, p = 0.24, Wilcoxon rank-sum test) or the vestibular condition (naive ... 17.4 spks/s versus trained ... 17.2 spks/s, p = 0.36)
outcomes.notes: As fig4-tuning-width-visual.

outcomes.statement: Neurons preferring lateral headings are more sensitive to heading variation around straight ahead than neurons preferring fore-aft headings (p << 0.001, factorial ANOVA).
outcomes.source: Results, Effects of Training on Tuning Curves, Variability, and Sensitivity of Single Neurons, paragraph 3; Figures 4C, 4D, 4G and 4H
outcomes.quote: lateral neurons were significantly more sensitive than fore-aft neurons for heading discrimination around straight ahead (p << 0.001, Factorial ANOVA, Figures 4D and 4H)

statistics.test: factorial ANOVA, main effect of preference group

outcomes.notes: On 258 values from 129 units of two trained monkeys, lateral units have lower median thresholds than fore-aft ones under every reading, in both conditions. Under one of the 8 readings of the claims file the difference reaches p < 0.001, as the criterion requires ("under one reading"), with vector-sum preference, spline threshold, log10, condition as a factor, p = 1.9e-07. Per condition that reading gives visual p = 3.4e-07 and vestibular p = 0.040, so the per-condition reading fails in the vestibular condition. In the other 7 readings the two-factor p is 0.013 to 0.77, and with spline-peak preferences no reading reaches p < 0.05. The neurometric thresholds of experiment 2, a variant, give two-factor p = 7.3e-07 (vector sum, log10) and 0.0011 (spline peak, log10). Per monkey, the visual difference is significant in both (p = 0.00024 and 0.00017) and the vestibular one in neither (p = 0.082 and 0.185). The outcome rests on the one passing reading. In it the preference by condition interaction is significant (p = 0.026), the difference being larger in the visual condition. The two-factor ANOVA counts each unit twice; a mixed model with a random intercept per unit gives p = 2.7e-07 in that reading and no other reading below 0.001. With a proxy of the paper's tuning selection, 252 of 258 values are kept and the reading gives p = 1.2e-07 (mixed model 1.8e-07); with a stricter proxy, 169 are kept and it gives p = 9.6e-08. Under both, no other reading reaches p < 0.001 (smallest 0.012), and the smallest two-factor p with spline-peak preferences is 0.051. Tested after the round-1 verification found that the claim had been blocked wrongly.
deviations: A subset of the paper's data. The experiment 1 tuning curves hold 129 units of two trained monkeys (Gu et al. 2008), against the paper's 992 visual and 556 vestibular neurons of naive and trained animals, so the ANOVA has no training factor. The two-factor reading has preference group and condition.

For the linear interpolation the derivative at 0, a sampled heading, is the slope between -22.5 and 22.5 degrees, a choice made here as a piecewise-linear curve has no derivative at a knot. Two values whose curve is flat at 0 have infinite thresholds and are left out of that reading.

The tuning curves in spikes/s are read as counts over the middle 1 s (Experimental Procedures, Noise and Signal Correlations). The first term of equation 3 scales with the window and the trace term does not, so another window does not scale all thresholds alike; with 0.5 s or 2 s the passing reading gives p = 1.9e-07, as with 1 s.

The Figure 4 legend includes only neurons with significant heading tuning (p < 0.05, ANOVA). That selection needs trial responses, which the data set does not hold, so the readings include every unit. As a check, a proxy selection computes the one-way ANOVA from each mean curve with variance equal to the mean (equation 4) and five repetitions ("typically repeated five times", Experimental Protocol and Task), and a stricter one with three repetitions and variance twice the mean; the outcome is the same under both.
The two-factor reading counts each unit once per condition; a mixed model with a random intercept per unit is shown and agrees.
The vector sum weights each response by the angle it covers, as in fig8ab.

outcomes.statement: Neuronal sensitivity does not differ between naive and trained animals for either fore-aft or lateral neurons (p > 0.5, factorial ANOVA), with no interaction (p > 0.3).
outcomes.source: Results, Effects of Training on Tuning Curves, Variability, and Sensitivity of Single Neurons, paragraph 3; Figures 4D and 4H
outcomes.quote: neuronal sensitivity was not significantly different between naive and trained animals (p > 0.5, factorial ANOVA) for either group of neurons, with no significant interaction effect (p > 0.3)

statistics.about: interaction of training and preference group

outcomes.notes: Needs naive single units, which the data set does not hold; the trained units are tested under fig4dh-lateral-more-sensitive.

outcomes.statement: Population sensitivity computed from the single-electrode database does not differ between naive and trained animals at any reference heading; the bootstrap 95% confidence bands largely overlap.
outcomes.source: Results, Effects of Training on Tuning Curves, Variability, and Sensitivity of Single Neurons, paragraph 3; Figure S4
outcomes.quote: Confidence intervals are largely overlapping between naïve (blue) and trained (pink) animals
outcomes.notes: Needs the naive and trained single-electrode database; only 129 trained units are in the data set.

outcomes.statement: Decoding real MSTd pairs, the ratio of thresholds with rnoise = 0.1 and rnoise = 0 rises above 1 for pairs with positive signal correlation and falls below 1 for negative signal correlation (R = 0.49, p << 0.001, Spearman).
outcomes.source: Results, Effect of Training on Population Coding Efficiency, paragraph 3; Figure 7B
outcomes.quote: pairs of neurons with positive rsignal yield discrimination thresholds that increase with rnoise, whereas pairs with negative rsignal have discrimination thresholds that decrease with rnoise (R = 0.49, p << 0.001, Spearman rank correlation)
outcomes.notes: Needs the tuning curves of each pair's units; the pairs carry only rsignal and preferred headings. Seven pairs, each in its own recording, share a cell id with experiment 1 units (printed under the data check), but the data set does not say which pair unit, if any, those curves belong to.

outcomes.statement: Noise correlation differs between naive and trained animals (p = 0.008) but is not affected by the congruency of the two units (p > 0.5), with no interaction (p > 0.5), two-way ANOVA; an ANCOVA finds no effect of congruency on the relation to signal correlation.
outcomes.source: Results, Training Effects on the Noise-Signal Correlation Structure, paragraph 3; Figure S5
outcomes.quote: While the average noise correlation was significantly different between 'naïve' (blue bars) and 'trained' (red bars) animals (p=0.008, main effect of training, two-way ANOVA), it was not significantly affected by the congruency of the two units in each pair (p>0.5, main effect of congruency, two-way ANOVA)

statistics.about: congruency in the ANCOVA with rsignal
interaction of congruency with rsignal in the ANCOVA
interaction of congruency with training group in the ANCOVA

outcomes.notes: The congruency index is the correlation of each unit's visual and vestibular tuning curves, which the data set does not hold for the pair units.

outcomes.statement: For 41 pairs recorded in both tasks, noise correlations during fixation and during heading discrimination are correlated (R = 0.47, p = 0.002) and their means do not differ (p = 0.26, paired t test).
outcomes.source: Results, Computation of Covariance Matrix, paragraph 2; Figure S6
outcomes.quote: Noise correlations were significantly correlated across task conditions (R=0.47, p=0.002, Spearman rank correlation) and the mean values were not significantly different (p=0.26, paired t-test, n=41)
outcomes.notes: Noise correlations during the discrimination task are not in the data set.

outcomes.statement: Naive animals fixate as accurately as trained animals and make fewer microsaccades (p << 0.001, t test).
outcomes.source: Discussion, Possible Explanations for the Effect of Training on Correlated Noise, paragraph 2; Figures S8A and S8B
outcomes.quote: we found that naive animals fixate as accurately as trained animals (Figure S8A). Indeed, naive monkeys as a group made significantly fewer microsaccades than trained animals (Figure S8B)
outcomes.notes: Eye position records are not in the data set.

findings.statement: The data set holds derived values only. For the paper's pairs there are no spike times or trial responses, no interneuronal distances, none of the 52 pairs over 1 mm, no discrimination-task correlations and no eye records; the single-electrode database of Figures 4, S4 and 8A is represented only by 129 units of two trained monkeys, and the training histories of Figure 2A by one threshold for each of two monkeys. Eighteen of the 35 claims cannot be tested.

No pair or monkey carries a naive or trained label, which every comparison in the paper needs. The groups can be recovered here only because the paper's per-animal pair counts are all distinct and match the counts per monkey in the file_ids.

No pair carries an electrode or distance label, and ten pairs of monkey 17, in six recordings (m17c36r1s, m17c40r1s, m17c41r1s, m17c42r1s, m17c44r1s, m17c48r1s), have file_ids ending in "s" without explanation, so the single-electrode and multi-electrode pairs cannot be told apart.

The data descriptor does not say how heading_pref was computed, how cp is signed (relative to the unit's preferred direction or to a fixed choice), or the units of resp_global (demo.m labels them spikes/s).

The data descriptor lists monkeys 1, 2, 3, 5, 17, 18 and 19 for the 127 MSTd pairs; the file_ids name an eighth, monkey 24, with two pairs, the trained animal with two pairs of the paper's Figure S2B.
Recording m19c21r1 holds six pairs from four units, where the paper states a maximum of five pairs in an experiment (Experimental Procedures, Electrophysiological Recordings).

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 1. The first executed notebook with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper. The verifier checked the archive listing for the blocked claims and tested the helper functions on synthetic inputs (tls_plane, threshold, sigma_for_fwhm, preference_group, pref_spline_peak, pref_vector_sum, pooled_rnoise). Report in transcripts/crcns-stc-1/verifier-1-report.md.

disagreements.reason: The proportions are 48.6, 73.1 and 92.4%, all within tolerance, and the improvement grows from -0.5% to about 4.8%. The best improvement of 4.83% is far outside 8 +- 0.8. It stays at 3.6 to 6.0% under the amplitude and baseline variants; only dropping the trace term, which is not equation 3, reaches 8%.

Blocked wrongly. Its main claim is the preference-group effect, which can be tested within the two trained monkeys from experiment1 and experiment2, with the claims-file Fisher threshold on interpolated tuning curves; the notebook used exactly this subset for fig8ab. The claim should be partially tested, not blocked (problem 2).

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 2. The full executed notebook with the conclusions and the summary, the attempt record, the README, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper. Report in transcripts/crcns-stc-1/verifier-2-report.md. Points not tied to one claim, the README's "It takes about two minutes" (no output gives a run time) is answered by a cell before the summary that prints the run time (51 s), and the README now says about one minute.

paper_notes.statement: Question for the paper's authors. Is the pooled rnoise of Figure 2B and Figure 5 the correlation of z-scores pooled over both conditions (which the mean of the two per-condition values in the data set approximates, giving 0.0241 and 0.1190, within the SEMs of the paper's 0.023 and 0.116), and do the stored per-condition values include the renormalization in blocks of 20 trials?

Question for the paper's authors. What tuning amplitude, baseline and counting window were used in the simulations of Figures 6 and 7, and was the trace term of equation 3 included? With amplitude 30 and baseline 10 spikes/s over 1 s and the trace term, the naive threshold is 5.4 times the independent one at 2000 neurons, but the best trained improvement in Figure 7C is 4.8%, not 8%; without the trace term it is 9.2 times and up to 11.8%.

Question for the paper's authors. How were the 95% intervals of the intercepts in Figure 5D computed? Separate per-group fits, the ANCOVA model with interaction and the common-slope model all give overlapping intervals on the 127 pairs of the data set.

Question for the paper's authors. For Figure 8A and 8B, how was each unit's preferred heading computed, which units entered the 311 values, and how was CP signed? On the 129 units of the data set neither the vector sum nor the spline peak gives fore-aft CPs smaller than lateral ones (p = 0.80 and 0.14).

entries.name: gu-2011
entries.title: Perceptual learning and noise correlations in MSTd (Gu et al. 2011)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Gu, Liu, Fetsch, Yang, Fok, Sunkara, DeAngelis and Angelaki (2011) on CRCNS stc-1, which holds the noise and signal correlations and preferred headings of the paper's 127 MSTd pairs under 1 mm, and single-unit tuning and choice probabilities of two trained monkeys. It compares noise correlations between naive and trained animals, their relation to signal correlation, and the paper's population simulations. Analyses that need spike times, distances or the single-electrode database cannot be run on it.
